The alto clarinet belongs to the clarinet family, a transposing woodwind aerophone in E♭, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.211.2. Its body is thick and straight, made of African blackwood, hard rubber, plastic or metal, with a curved neck and a metal bell. It is usually held on a shoulder strap; the fingering is close to the clarinet's, and the Boehm or Oehler system is common. It appears mainly in wind bands and clarinet choirs, a few jazz players use it, and it is less common in the orchestra.

Grainger's wind-band piece Lincolnshire Posy has a famous solo; Stravinsky used the instrument in F in Threni and the one in E♭ in Elegy for J.F.K.; Holbrooke's Second Symphony Apollo and the Seamen has an important part. Gatta also wrote an orchestral concerto for it.

Its principle is the same as the clarinet's, with a thicker low register, and the top can be helped by the half-hole key. Because the body is wider and the volume weaker than the clarinet's, it usually relies on a larger, umbrella-shaped bell to amplify and project the sound. Beside the alto saxophone its timbre is more focused; beside the basset horn its range is narrower and its key lower.

The modern alto clarinet is mostly credited to the German makers Iwan Müller and Grenser; in 1809 Müller already had a sixteen-key instrument in F, when the soprano clarinet usually had only ten to twelve keys. An anonymous E♭ instrument also appeared in the United States around 1820, shaped like a bassoon but fingered like a clarinet, close to the patent clarion, the bass clarinet that George Catlin built at Hartford, Connecticut from about 1810. Adolphe Sax later improved it in Europe. In the mid twentieth century there was discussion of removing it from the wind band, and its use declined for a time, but modern wind bands and clarinet choirs still keep it.

The fingering is mostly the Boehm system: the keys sit in much the same places as on the clarinet, but there is usually one more key, which gives a lower written note. Because it is in E♭ the fingering and the way of sounding are close to the soprano clarinet's, while the actual pitch is an octave lower. It is written in treble clef and sounds a major sixth below the written pitch. Beginners should first master reading transposed notation, the key positions and the shoulder strap, then work through the notes of the range.
